sources.news_title: Georgian Picture O'Keeffe Found in Apartment Closet Will Be Auctioned for up to R$ 28 Million
sources.text:
Quadro de Georgia O'Keeffe encontrado em armário de apartamento será leiloado por até R$ 28 milhões
Obra de 1930 estava escondida havia décadas atrás de casacos e caixas em imóvel de Nova York; pintura de paisagem do Novo México foi avaliada em até US$ 5 milhões pela Christie's
Por O Globo — Nova York
Atualizado
Uma pintura da artista americana Georgia O'Keeffe, escondida durante décadas no armário de um apartamento em Manhattan, Nova York, será leiloada por até US$ 5 milhões (cerca de R$ 28 milhões). A obra, produzida em 1930, foi encontrada atrás de casacos e caixas durante a organização dos pertences de uma mulher que morreu recentemente, aos quase 100 anos. Segundo informações divulgadas pela emissora ABC News, poucos familiares sabiam da existência do quadro até que a antiga proprietária comentou casualmente com uma sobrinha que tinha uma obra de O'Keeffe guardada no armário.
- Escritor e ex-vice da Nicarágua, Sergio Ramírez toma posse na Real Academia Espanhola, em vaga de Vargas Llosa
- Veja também: Herdeiros judeus contestam venda de pintura de Van Gogh avaliada em mais de R$ 1 bilhão
A pintura retrata o Lobo Peak, uma montanha próxima à cidade de Taos, no estado americano do Novo México, com colinas em tons terrosos. A casa de leilões Christie's estima o valor da peça entre US$ 3 milhões e US$ 5 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 16 milhões a R$ 28 milhões). O leilão está previsto para esta terça-feira (17).
Obra ficou desaparecida por décadas
De acordo com a Christie's, a pintura foi vendida em 1963 por uma galeria de arte de Nova York por US$ 3.800 a uma mulher que posteriormente a deu à filha. A família acredita que a obra tenha sido um presente de formatura, depois que a jovem concluiu um mestrado na década de 1960.
A proprietária manteve o quadro exposto em seu apartamento no East Village por vários anos. Em meados da década de 1980, porém, decidiu guardá-lo na embalagem original, depois de perceber que um visitante demonstrava interesse excessivo pela pintura. Desde então, a obra permaneceu escondida no armário.
Por volta de 2022, a mulher comentou pela primeira vez com a sobrinha que havia uma pintura de Georgia O'Keeffe guardada no imóvel. O quadro só foi retirado da embalagem neste ano, durante a organização do apartamento e dos pertences da antiga proprietária.
A família pediu que suas identidades não fossem divulgadas. Segundo a sobrinha, que ajudou a cuidar da mulher nos últimos anos, ela era extremamente reservada, nunca se casou e trabalhou durante um período no Serviço de Relações Exteriores dos Estados Unidos, com passagens pela Europa.
Pintura tem importância histórica
A obra é considerada particularmente relevante por representar o início da relação de O'Keeffe com as paisagens do sudoeste americano. Segundo Tylee Abbott, diretor de Arte Americana da Christie's, a pintura provavelmente foi a primeira de uma série de três.
A segunda versão está no acervo do Metropolitan Museum of Art, em Nova York. A terceira pertenceu durante muitos anos à coleção da família Rockefeller. A localização da primeira obra, por sua vez, era praticamente desconhecida até a descoberta no apartamento.
Antes de ser vendida em 1963, a pintura era conhecida principalmente por meio de fotografias feitas em 1931, segundo Abbott.
Museu nos EUA gera debate ético por expor restos mortais humanos
A autenticidade foi confirmada após a retirada da embalagem. Entre os elementos que ajudaram na identificação está uma marca característica da artista no verso da tela: uma estrela com as iniciais "OK" escritas no centro.
Quem foi Georgia O'Keeffe?
Considerada uma das pioneiras do modernismo americano, Georgia O'Keeffe (1887-1986) ficou conhecida por desenvolver uma linguagem artística própria, com pinturas abstratas, flores em grandes dimensões e paisagens do sudoeste dos Estados Unidos.
A artista passou boa parte da vida no Novo México, onde construiu uma casa e um estúdio em Abiquiú. As paisagens desérticas da região tiveram papel importante em sua produção artística.
Conhecida como a "mãe do modernismo americano", O'Keeffe morreu em 1986, aos 98 anos, deixando um legado que a consolidou como uma das figuras mais importantes da arte moderna nos Estados Unidos.

sources.news_title: A Georgia O’Keeffe painting was buried in a New York apartment closet. It is going up for auction. - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
NEW YORK — The painting was buried behind coats and boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades.
Few if anyone knew about the hidden treasure until the woman in her 90s who lived there nonchalantly told her niece one day, “Oh by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
The painting — an early example from a time when O’Keeffe became enamored with the American Southwest — depicts a classic New Mexico landscape with rolling hills in earth tones.
Christie’s estimates its value at $3 million to $5 million. It is set to go up for auction on Tuesday.
The auction house says the painting from 1930 was likely the first in a series of three. The second is in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.
Up until now, the whereabouts of the first one had largely been a mystery.
O’Keeffe painting comes from a key period
The painting of Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico, is “particularly important because of its early date and its representation of the inception point of O’Keeffe’s time in the American Southwest,” said Tylee Abbott, director of American Art at Christie’s.
In 1963, a New York art gallery sold the painting for $3,800 to a woman who gave it to her daughter.
“Before that it was only known through photography that had been taken in 1931,” Abbott said.
O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at age 98, is often called the “Mother of American modernism.” She was a pioneer with her own style of abstract art, most known for paintings of flowers and Southwestern landscapes.
She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio on land with breathtaking desert vistas that inspired the work of the 20th century painter. Many Native American communities trace their ancestry to the area in northern New Mexico.
Family believes painting was a graduation gift
The daughter of the woman who purchased the painting in 1963 kept it at her apartment in New York’s East Village, the auction house said. The family has asked the auction house not to release their identities.
But they did share with Christie’s some details, including how the artwork was found.
The woman who owned the painting lived into her late 90s before dying recently. Never married, she was extremely private and incredibly smart, the family said. At one point in her life, she worked with the US Foreign Service, spending time in Europe.
She collected antiques and abstract art but nothing close to the stature of the O’Keeffe.
The family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother after earning a master’s degree in the 1960s. For many years, she displayed it until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely.
Painting has O’Keeffe’s signature mark
She boxed it back into the original packing crate and put it in the back of a closet, said her niece, who spent the last few years caring for her and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to honor the family’s request for privacy.
Around 2022, the woman first mentioned to her niece that the painting was in the front closet. It stayed there until this year when they were cleaning out the apartment and getting her affairs in order.
Once unboxed, it was obvious the painting was authentic.
It has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work — including her signature marking on the back, a star with her initials “OK” scrawled in the middle.
Seewer reported from Ohio.

sources.news_title: Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found in New York Apartment Closet Heads to Auction
sources.text:
NEW YORK – For decades, the painting sat unnoticed beneath coats and cardboard boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment.
Almost no one knew the artwork was there until its owner, a woman in her 90s, casually mentioned to her niece one day: “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
The work, an early painting from the period when O’Keeffe became captivated by the American Southwest, portrays a quintessential New Mexico landscape of rolling, earth-toned hills.
Christie’s has placed its estimated value at $3 million to $5 million. The painting is scheduled to be auctioned Tuesday.
According to the auction house, the 1930 painting was probably the first of a three-work series. The second is held by New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, while the third spent many years in the collection of the Rockefeller family.
Until its rediscovery, the first painting’s location had been largely unknown.
O’Keeffe painting emerges
from a pivotal period
The painting depicts Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico. Its significance lies “particularly” in its early date and its depiction of the beginnings of O’Keeffe’s relationship with the American Southwest, said Tylee Abbott, Christie’s director of American Art.
A New York gallery sold the work for $3,800 in 1963 to a woman who later gave it to her daughter.
Before that sale, Abbott said, the painting was known only through a photograph taken in 1931.
O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at 98, is widely regarded as the “Mother of American modernism.” A trailblazer with a distinctive approach to abstraction, she became especially known for her flower paintings and depictions of the Southwest.
She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio surrounded by the sweeping desert views that shaped much of her work. The region in northern New Mexico is also ancestral homeland to many Native American communities.
Family believes painting was a graduation gift
The daughter of the woman who bought the painting in 1963 kept it in her New York East Village apartment, Christie’s said. At the family’s request, the auction house has not disclosed their identities.
They did, however, provide Christie’s with details about the painting’s long-hidden history and eventual discovery.
The owner lived into her late 90s and died recently. She never married and was described by relatives as intensely private and exceptionally intelligent. During her career with the U.S. Foreign Service, she spent time in Europe.
She collected antiques and abstract art, though none of the pieces in her collection approached the stature of the O’Keeffe.
The family suspects she received the painting as a graduation present from her mother after completing a master’s degree in the 1960s. She displayed it for years, but in the mid-1980s noticed a guest paying unusually close attention to the work.
Painting bears O’Keeffe’s signature mark
Her niece said the owner placed the painting back in its original shipping crate and stored it at the rear of a closet. The niece, who cared for her during the final years of her life, spoke with The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to respect the family’s privacy.
Around 2022, the woman told her niece for the first time that the painting was in the front closet. It remained there until this year, when the family began clearing out the apartment and handling her affairs.
When the painting was finally removed from its crate, its authenticity quickly became apparent.
The work bears the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s art, including a distinctive signature mark on the reverse: a star with her initials, “OK,” written at its center.
___
Seewer reported from Ohio.

sources.news_title: Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Heads to Auction
sources.text:
NEW YORK – For decades, the painting sat hidden beneath coats and boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment.
Almost no one knew the artwork was there until its owner, a woman in her 90s, casually mentioned to her niece one day: “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
The painting is an early work from the period when O’Keeffe became captivated by the American Southwest. It portrays a quintessential New Mexico landscape, with rolling hills rendered in warm earth tones.
Christie’s has estimated the painting’s value at $3 million to $5 million. It is scheduled to be offered at auction Tuesday.
The auction house says the 1930 painting was probably the first of a series of three. The second is held by New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, while the third belonged for many years to the Rockefeller family.
Until now, the location of the first painting had remained largely unknown.
O’Keeffe painting comes from a key period
The work depicts Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico. It is “particularly important because of its early date and its representation of the inception point of O’Keeffe’s time in the American Southwest,” said Tylee Abbott, Christie’s director of American Art.
A New York art gallery sold the painting for $3,800 in 1963 to a woman who later gave it to her daughter.
“Before that it was only known through photography that had been taken in 1931,” Abbott said.
O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at age 98, is widely regarded as the “Mother of American modernism.” A pioneer who developed a distinctive abstract style, she is best known for paintings of flowers and Southwestern landscapes.
She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio surrounded by sweeping desert views that influenced her work as a 20th-century painter. The region in northern New Mexico is also the ancestral homeland of many Native American communities.
Family believes painting was a graduation gift
The daughter of the woman who bought the painting in 1963 kept it in her East Village apartment, according to the auction house. The family has asked Christie’s not to disclose its identity.
They did, however, provide the auction house with details about the artwork, including the story of how it was rediscovered.
The painting’s owner lived into her late 90s and died recently. She never married and was described by her family as deeply private and exceptionally intelligent. During her career, she worked for the U.S. Foreign Service and spent time in Europe.
She collected antiques and abstract art, though nothing else in her collection approached the significance of the O’Keeffe.
The family believes her mother gave her the painting as a graduation present after she completed a master’s degree in the 1960s. She displayed it for years, but in the mid-1980s became concerned after noticing a guest paying unusually close attention to it.
Painting bears O’Keeffe’s signature mark
The woman placed the painting back in its original packing crate and stored it at the rear of a closet, her niece said. The niece spent the last several years caring for her aunt and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to respect the family’s privacy.
Around 2022, the woman first told her niece that the painting was in the front closet. It remained there until this year, when the family began clearing out the apartment and settling her affairs.
Once the artwork was removed from its crate, its authenticity was apparent.
The painting contains all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her distinctive signature mark on the back: a star with her initials, “OK,” written in the center.
___
Seewer reported from Ohio.
